newsitem.title: UK: UK pollsters await election moment of truth.
newsitem.headline: UK pollsters await election moment of truth.

text.p: It is not just Britain's politicians who nervously await the people's verdict at next week's election.
The nation's much-maligned opinion pollsters will find out on May 2, the day after the election when the result become clear, just how closely their predictions were to reality.

The huge range in current polls suggest that some polling organisations may be as far, or even further, out of line as they were in 1992 when they forecast a Labour victory and were pilloried as the Conservatives swept in with a 21-seat majority.
Two polls, published on Wednesday, showed why pollsters are rather nervous at the moment.
In the Guardian, ICM forecast a dramatic narrowing of the gap between the ruling Conservatives and the opposition Labour to just five points from 14 points a week ago.
But the Telegraph's "rolling poll", conducted by Gallup every 24 hours, showed Labour had a lead over the Conservatives of 21 points, scarcely different from its findings a week ago.
Even factoring in a margin for error of around three percentage points, the results tell hugely different stories.
ICM's Nick Sparrow said he was confident of the methods used in the maverick Guardian poll.

"There is no perfect way to conduct a poll, it is a choice between imperfect alternatives," Sparrow told Reuters. "But if there had been any doubt at all about this poll, I would not have allowed the findings to be published."
Independent poll experts said that at first sight, ICM had come up with a rogue poll, something which is expected to happen about once in every 20 surveys.

"I think the best judgment is that it is a rogue poll, although there may be an indication that the Labour lead is narrowing a little bit," said political scientist John Curtice of the University of Strathclyde in Glasgow.
Anthony King, professor of government at the University of Essex, wrote in the Telegraph that it was possible that ICM could have picked up a new trend.
"Only more surveys in the next few days will settle the issue. In the meantime, no one should allow themselves to get over-excited, great though the temptation will be on both sides," he said.
A panel of top voting experts, now polled by Reuters on a weekly basis, gives a further illustration of how election forecasting is more an art than a science.
In the panel's latest findings, published on Wednesday, the experts put the average Labour lead at nine points, with 44 percent of the vote compared with the Conservatives' 35 percent.
But the range of predictions was enormous, from one forecasting a hung parliament with no overall majority, to another who thinks Labour will have a 179-seat majority.
Unless some experts make dramatic adjustments to their predictions in the next week, some will end up badly wrong.
Stung by the criticism they attracted in 1992, polling organisations are using different methods in their bid to construct the perfect poll.
Some have changed to telephone sampling, while others have stuck to the age-old method of face-to-face interviews.

Then they use different statistical adjustments for inconclusive data, particularly in the hazy realm of the "don't knows" and those who refuse to answer, who make up around one quarter of those questioned in some polls.
A trend of "shy" Tories -- voters who do not like to admit openly to interviewers that they support the Conservative party -- is now so well-known that it tends to be factored into adjusted results.

The eccentricities of Britain's voting system, which makes just a few thousand votes in marginal constituencies across the country pivotal to the outcome, further confound the best efforts of the pollsters.
"There is only one certainty. We will find out who's right next week," said ICM's Sparrow.
